div.head: Many researches o n dynamic scheduling techniques for real-time systems have focused o n changes in the number of tasks. I n this paper we propose a dynamic real-time scheduling technique, called M A R T , in which it is also possible to change task characteristics. W h e n M A R T is used
div.p: in systems where task characteristics need to be and can be modified, it enables the system to be adaptable to changing environments dynamically and flexibly. B y using M A R T , systems can accept on-line requirements such as changing task timing characteristics, and adding OT deleting tasks. If a task set becomes unschedulable as a result of such modifications, M A R T can determine a schedulable task set. Though M A R T must adjust timing characteristics of other tasks to guarantee the schedulability of all tasks, the need for such adjustments is reduced.

W e also argue the importance of predictabdaty in realtime compzlting, then improve the predictability of M A R T by introducing the notion of importance into each task. M A R T uses "inportance" as a factor for task characteristic adjustment.

div.head: Dynamic Features in Real-Time Systems
div.p: In this section, we claim that there are two kinds of dynamic features in real-time systems. One is addition and deletion of tasks and the other is changes of task characteristics.

div.head: Addition and deletion of tasks
div.p: This is the dynamic feature discussed commonly. This means that the number of tasks in a system changes dynamically.

div.head: Changes of task characteristics
div.p: This is the other dynamic feature which is merely discussed. Task characteristics, such as task execution time or resource requirement are changed. To clarify our motivation, we present both dynamic features with "video conference systems" as an example (Figure 1).

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In today's highly information-oriented society, realtime processing technologies are indispensable. Furthermore, in the next decade, computing environments will become more widely distributed. Along with such perspective, we have constructed a new programming paradigm [9][10].

Concerning the real-time scheduling, many works deal with static systems where behaviors of all tasks can be analyzed. Scheduling analysis of dynamic realtime systems have been generally considered to be extremely difficult, although its importance has been recognized.

'Also with Sony Computer Science Laboratory Inc. 3-14-13 Higashi-Gotanda, Shinagawa-ku, Tokyo, 141, Japan Fax+81-45-560-1151 In this paper, we point out that there are two kinds of dynamic features in real-time systems and claim that dynamic systems should be able to manage both features to construct systems which are adaptable to environmental changes flexibly (Section 2).

To realize the dynamic systems described above, we propose a scheduling technique MART which is acronym for Modification and Adjustment of Realtime Tasks. MART can accept requests, such as modifying the number of tasks, from an application to adapt environmental changes. Though, task periods may need to be adjusted to assure schedulability of all tasks, it is designed to reduce the amount of adjustments as little as possible (Section 3).

Predictability is another important property in real-time systems. It is difficult to support predictability in dynamic real-time systems. Especially, since MART adjusts task timing characteristics frequently, to guarantee the predictability is very difficult. So we introduce the notion of importance to tasks in order to support the predictability and evaluate the effectiveness in a simulation (Section 4).

Here, participants are distributed and are displayed on all participants' system monitors (Figure l A process of video data sent at crfP~(frames per second) is regarded as a periodic real-time task whose period is l/a sec. Execution time of each task is determined by its portrait size and resolution.

Someone participates or leaves the conference in the middle of it. These situations correspond to the addition and deletion of tasks. Moreover when someone begins speech, the window size or the frame rate to display him should be increased. These situations are correspond t o the changes of task characteristics.

Hence, we have to consider both of dynamic features in real-time systems: addition and deletion of tasks and changes of task taming characteristics, although there are few scheduling techniques which deal with these features. If the system always accepts requests, such as addition of tasks, from an application, it is obvious that the task set becomes unschedulable some time. In this case, rejecting the requests is one of the solutions to maintain schedulability of all the tasks. However, to construct highly flexible systems, such as video conference systems, it is necessary to develop a new scheduling technique which can satisfy both requirements, the modifications of task set and the maintenance of schedulability of all the tasks. In this strategy, unfortunately, we have to adjust timing characteristics of all tasks to keep up schedulability of the task set. Therefore, in this paper, we focus on the systems which are composed of tasks whose timing characteristics need to be and can be changed dynamically.
Based on the above discussion, we present requirements for a practical design of video conference systems.

The scheduling algorithms for real-time systems which support dynamic changes are discussed in [2] [4][6] [8]. In particular, the algorithm proposed by Mok et al. [6] is for highly flexibile dynamic real-time systems which need to modify task timing characteristics according to environmental changes. Their motivation is very similar to ours. However, since task addition or deletion is not considered, and the ratio of each task's execution time and period are kept constant, thus their method cannot be used for the application which is described in this paper. Sha et al. [8] consider task addition and deletion, and changing task period and execution time. However they change task timing characteristics to control priority, not to adapt to environmental changes dynamically, so it does not meet our requirements.

div.head: MART
div.p: MART, which follows the steps described in Section 2, enable us constructing a system capable of modifying the number of tasks or task timing characteristics according to environment changes. The most important characteristic of MART is that it always maintains schedulability of a task set under the rate monotonic scheduling algorithm.

div.head: System Model and Terminology
div.p: MART assumes the following system model.
All tasks are periodic. Deadlines are presented by periods. Tasks are independent and preemptive. Modification of task execution time and period are allowed.
e Addition and deletion of tasks are allowed.

In this paper, we distinguish the terms, modification and adjustment as follows: Modification . . . Task addition/deletion or changes of task timing characteristics occur as a result of an acceptance of a request from applications.
Adjustment . . -Alteration of a task period to restore schedulability. It is applied when the task set becomes unschedulable as a result of a modification as described above.

div.head: Rate Monotonic Scheduling Algorit hm
div.p: The rate monotonic scheduling algorithm is a static, preemptive and fixed priority scheduling algorithm for periodic tasks. It gives higher priority to shorter period tasks[3]. This algorithm features clear and easy analysis of schedulability. Thus, we focus on this algorithm. Let n be the number of tasks, Ci the execution time, and Ti the period of task T*. div.head: Outline of MART
div.p: MART can accept four kinds of requests; modification of a task execution time, modification of a task period, scheduling of a newly created task, and deletion of a task. After the system accepts one of these requests, MART first analyzes the schedulability of the task set. If it becomes unschedulable due to a modification described above, the periods of some tasks are adjusted to restore its schedulability2. If it remains schedulable after the system has accepted a request, it preserves present conditions. 'There are some other ways that can be taken for adjustments. For example, it is possible to shorten execution time. We plan to examine these in future works.

div.head: Overload
div.p: If a system is under unpredictable transient overload, task deadlines may be missed in reverse order of priorities under the rate monotonic scheduling algorithm. In MART, priorities are changed along with the adjustment of task periods. Unfortunately, with the strategy given in Section 3, it is difficult to analyze which tasks may miss their deadline under transient overload a t runtime.

In real-time systems, runtime behaviors of tasks had better be analyzable for system designers. There are various ways to define predictability according to "how and what can we predict?"[l]. In this paper, we define predictable systems as follows:

div.head: Definition 4.1 Predictable Systems Predictable systems are defined as systems that can analyze the task which may not meet its deadline when the systems are under transient overload.
div.p: In this section, we introduce the notion of importance into tasks to construct the predictable systems with MART.

div.head: MART with Importance
div.p: MART is based on the rate monotonic scheduling algorithm. So, to make a predictable system described above means that the tasks having a long period in the system are always analyzable while the application is running. Task importance means "semantic importance".
They are not always equal to task priorities. It is used as a factor in adjustment of period, so users can determine which task is important in the application with the importance.

div.head: Evaluation of Predictability
div.p: We evaluate the improvement of predictability by introducing importance though simulations. In the simulations, to simplify discussion, we assume that the system can only accept two kinds of requests, i.e. to modify the execution time and to modify the period. And we used random numbers t o determine task id, either new value of execution time or period, for the task set shown in Section 3.5. So, t o introduce importance to tasks is an effective way to construct predictable systems. Table 2 also shows that if we use larger A, we can make more predictable systems.

Because, in the entry of task importance 3, the probability of A = 0.1 that importance and priority are in agreement is higher than that of A = 0.05. Consequently predictable systems as defined in this paper can be constructed with a high probability if we use MART with task importance.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we pointed out that there are two kinds of dynamic features in real-time systems and proposed a new scheduling technique MART which can construct highly flexible dynamic real-time systems. MART is based on the rate monotonic scheduling algorithm, and can accept application requests to modify the number of tasks or task timing characteristics to adapt t o environmental changes flexibly.

If the task set becomes unschedulable as a result of these modifications, MART keeps schedulability of the task set by adjusting task periods. Some task periods may be extended at this time, however MART is designed t o reduce the amount of adjustment as possible. MART aims to retain all tasks, even if quality of service of each task is somewhat reduced.

We also emphasized the importance of predictability in real-time computing. First, we defined predictable systems. Then, to improve the predictabil- ity, we introduced the notion of importance into tasks. Then, we evaluated the predictability through siniulation, and confirmed the efficiency of MART with importance.
We are currently interested in extending our technique to adjust task execution time. And, we also plan to implement and evaluate MART on real computer systems.
